1.description: Male cardinals brilliant red against deep snow, singing from bare branches even in bitter cold
1.childFriendlyNote: A bright red bird that looks like a flame sitting in the snow. He sings "cheer-cheer-cheer!" even when it's freezing

1.description: Chickadees visiting feeders in small flocks, calling "chick-a-dee-dee-dee" from bare branches
1.childFriendlyNote: A tiny brave bird that calls its own name ("chickadee-dee-dee!") even in the coldest weather

1.description: Fresh snow reveals tracks of rabbits, squirrels, deer, and foxes: a story of the night written in white
1.childFriendlyNote: After fresh snow, look for footprints. Can you figure out which animal walked here at night?

1.description: Deer browsing in groups near forest edges, pawing through deep snow for food
1.childFriendlyNote: Deer lift their big white tails like flags when they run. It warns the others "danger!"

1.description: Thick ice on ponds, frost ferns on windows, frozen streams with sculptural ice formations
1.childFriendlyNote: Look at frozen puddles. The ice makes fern and feather patterns like tiny fairy artwork

2.description: Male cardinals brilliant red against deep snow, singing from bare branches
2.childFriendlyNote: A bright red bird that looks like a flame sitting in the snow. He sings "cheer-cheer-cheer!"

2.description: Tufted titmice at feeders with chickadees, grey with a pointed crest and big dark eyes
2.childFriendlyNote: A little grey bird with a pointy hat and big eyes. It calls "peter-peter-peter!"

2.description: Red-tailed hawks perched on bare trees and telephone poles, hunting over snowy fields
2.childFriendlyNote: A big hawk sits on a pole watching for mice. When it flies you can see its rusty-red tail

2.description: Fresh snow reveals tracks of cottontail rabbits, grey squirrels, deer, and red foxes
2.childFriendlyNote: After fresh snow, look for footprints. Rabbit tracks look like exclamation marks!

2.description: Eastern white pine and hemlock standing green against grey winter sky, branches heavy with snow
2.childFriendlyNote: While other trees are bare, evergreen pines keep their needles all winter. Crush one and smell the fresh scent

3.description: Great horned owls courting and nesting. Listen for deep hooting duets at dusk, sometimes sitting on eggs with snow on their backs
3.childFriendlyNote: The biggest owl goes "hoo-hoo-hoooo" at night. They start nesting in the coldest month!

3.description: Chickadees visiting feeders in small flocks, their "fee-bee" song starting to be heard on warmer days
3.childFriendlyNote: Listen for "fee-bee". Chickadees start their spring song even when there's still snow everywhere

3.description: Male cardinals singing louder and longer as days lengthen, red against white snow
3.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal sings louder now. He's noticed the days getting a tiny bit longer!

3.description: Deep snow cover, ice thick on ponds, icicles forming on eaves: peak of New England winter
3.childFriendlyNote: This is when snow piles highest. Measure the snow depth with a stick and keep a chart!

3.description: Juncos foraging in flocks on snowy ground near feeders, flashing white outer tail feathers
3.childFriendlyNote: Little grey and white "snowbirds" hop around under feeders. They flash white tail feathers when they fly

4.description: Great horned owls incubating eggs. Listen for hooting duets at dusk near large nests in bare trees
4.childFriendlyNote: Mama owl is sitting on her eggs in the freezing cold. Papa owl brings her food

4.description: Cardinals singing at dawn, pairs beginning to form, red males courting brown females
4.childFriendlyNote: Mr Cardinal brings seeds to Mrs Cardinal. That's his way of saying "I like you!"

4.description: Tracks of cottontail rabbits, grey squirrels, and red foxes visible in fresh snow
4.childFriendlyNote: Fox tracks make a straight line, like stepping on a tightrope. Dogs zigzag all over!

4.description: Tufted titmice visiting feeders, beginning to sing their loud "peter-peter-peter" song
4.childFriendlyNote: A little grey bird with a pointy hat calls "peter-peter-peter!" from the treetops

4.description: Barred owls calling "who cooks for you, who cooks for you all" from deep woods at night
4.childFriendlyNote: This owl seems to ask "who cooks for you?". Listen for it in the woods after dark

5.description: Great horned owls on nests, sometimes visible in large bare trees. Look for ear tufts
5.childFriendlyNote: Can you spot the owl sitting on her nest? Look in big trees for a shape that doesn't belong

5.description: Chickadees singing "fee-bee" more frequently as days lengthen, still visiting feeders in flocks
5.childFriendlyNote: Listen for the sweet two-note "fee-bee". The chickadee is dreaming of spring!

5.description: Red-tailed hawks hunting over snowy fields, easily spotted perched on bare trees
5.childFriendlyNote: A big hawk sits on a pole watching for mice in the snow. Sharp eyes can spot a mouse from far away

5.description: Thick ice on ponds and lakes, sometimes with pressure cracks that boom and sing
5.childFriendlyNote: Frozen ponds make spooky booming sounds as the ice shifts. It's the lake talking!

5.description: Nuthatches walking headfirst down tree trunks, probing bark crevices for insects
5.childFriendlyNote: This bird walks down the tree trunk upside-down! It goes "yank-yank-yank!"

6.description: Cardinals singing more vigorously as February begins, staking out territories
6.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal sings louder every week now. He's picking his favourite tree to nest in

6.description: Great horned owl chicks may be hatching in nests, adults very territorial near nest sites
6.childFriendlyNote: Baby owls are hatching right now in the freezing cold! Their fluffy down keeps them warm

6.description: Chickadees singing "fee-bee" spring song on sunny mornings even though winter persists
6.childFriendlyNote: The chickadee knows spring is coming before we do. It sings "fee-bee" on sunny days

6.description: February often brings the heaviest snowfalls, snow banks piling up, icicles on eaves
6.childFriendlyNote: February can dump the most snow! Count the layers in a snow bank. Each one is a different storm

6.description: Downy woodpeckers drumming on trees, beginning territorial behaviour as days lengthen
6.childFriendlyNote: A tiny black and white bird hammers on trees like a little drummer, tap-tap-tap-tap!

7.description: Great horned owl chicks growing, adults hunting heavily to feed young
7.childFriendlyNote: Owl parents work hard to feed hungry babies. Listen for hooting at sunset

7.description: Red-tailed hawks beginning courtship flights, circling together over fields
7.childFriendlyNote: Two big hawks circle together in the sky, doing a slow dance in the air. They're falling in love

7.description: Chickadees singing "fee-bee" more often, flocks beginning to break into pairs
7.childFriendlyNote: Chickadee friends are pairing up, two by two instead of big groups

7.description: Cardinals singing at dawn, males feeding females as courtship intensifies
7.childFriendlyNote: Mr Cardinal brings seeds to Mrs Cardinal's beak. That's a bird kiss!

7.description: Tiny springtails (snow fleas) appearing on snow surface on warm days, look like pepper sprinkled on snow
7.childFriendlyNote: Tiny specks that jump on the snow! They're not really fleas: they're harmless little springtails

8.description: Cardinals singing vigorously at dawn, establishing nesting territories
8.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal is the earliest singer. He starts before the sun is even up!

8.description: Skunk cabbage beginning to push through frozen ground in wetlands, generates its own heat to melt through ice
8.childFriendlyNote: This plant is so warm it melts the snow around it! It smells terrible though, like a skunk!

8.description: Downy woodpeckers drumming loudly on resonant branches, territorial calls increasing
8.childFriendlyNote: Woodpeckers drum on the loudest branch they can find. It's like sending a text to other woodpeckers!

8.description: Crows gathering in large flocks, cawing from bare treetops as winter roosts begin to break up
8.childFriendlyNote: Big groups of crows meet every evening, hundreds of birds having a noisy sleepover!

8.description: Days noticeably longer than January: nearly 11 hours of daylight, sunset after 5:30pm
8.childFriendlyNote: Notice the sun is setting later? We're gaining about 2 minutes of daylight every day!

9.description: Skunk cabbage hoods pushing through snow and ice in swampy areas, dark mottled purple-green spathe visible
9.childFriendlyNote: Skunk cabbage melts its own snow cave! Its hood looks like a little gnome hat poking through ice

9.description: Crow flocks cawing from bare trees, winter roosts breaking up as pairs form
9.childFriendlyNote: Crows are the smartest birds around. They recognise human faces and share information!

9.description: Red-tailed hawks in courtship flights, soaring together and calling with a high screaming cry
9.childFriendlyNote: Hawks scream as they circle together. That high "keeee-ahhh" sound in movies is a red-tailed hawk!

9.description: Maple sap beginning to run on days above freezing followed by cold nights, sugar shacks firing up
9.childFriendlyNote: Sweet water starts dripping from maple trees. People collect it to boil into maple syrup!

9.description: Late February snow still deep across New England, but bright sun creating melt-freeze cycles
9.childFriendlyNote: The snow gets crunchy on top in the morning. It melts a little in the sun then refreezes at night

10.description: Peak maple sugaring season, sap running freely on warm days, sugar shacks steaming across the region
10.childFriendlyNote: Sweet water drips from maple trees into buckets. People boil it down to make maple syrup! It takes 40 gallons of sap for 1 gallon of syrup

10.description: Skunk cabbage hoods emerging strongly in wetlands, dark purple-brown spathes visible melting through remaining snow
10.childFriendlyNote: This amazing plant makes its own heat, warm enough to melt snow! But it smells like a skunk

10.description: Crows breaking into pairs, nest-building beginning in tall trees, still very vocal
10.childFriendlyNote: Crows carry sticks in their beaks. They're building nests high up in the tallest trees

10.description: First male red-winged blackbirds arriving at marshes, singing "conk-la-ree" even with snow on the ground
10.childFriendlyNote: A black bird flashes bright red shoulders and sings "conk-la-reee!" from the reeds, spring's first migrant!

10.description: March snowstorms still common in New England. Nor'easters can dump heavy wet snow
10.childFriendlyNote: March can still bring big snowstorms! But the snow melts faster now because the sun is stronger

11.description: Maple sugaring in full swing, buckets and tubing lines collecting sap, steam rising from sugar shacks
11.childFriendlyNote: Visit a sugar shack! The steam smells sweet and you can taste fresh maple syrup on snow

11.description: Male red-winged blackbirds claiming territories in marshes, singing loudly from cattails
11.childFriendlyNote: The blackbird puffs up his red shoulders to look tough: "this is my cattail!"

11.description: Skunk cabbage hoods fully emerged in wet areas, purple-brown spathes amid remaining snow patches
11.childFriendlyNote: More skunk cabbages popping up! Get close and smell it. Phew! It attracts flies for pollination

11.description: Pussy willows beginning to show fuzzy silver catkins along streams and wet areas
11.childFriendlyNote: Soft fuzzy buds on willow branches feel like tiny kittens. That's why they're called pussy willows!

11.description: First robins spotted, though many are actually overwintering birds becoming more visible as snow melts
11.childFriendlyNote: Is that a robin? Some stayed all winter hiding in the woods, but now they're coming out to lawns

12.description: Skunk cabbage hoods prominent in swamps and stream edges, green leaves beginning to unfurl inside the spathe
12.childFriendlyNote: The skunk cabbage hood is opening up and you can see green leaves curled inside, like a present unwrapping!

12.description: Male red-winged blackbirds singing from marshes and cattails, flashing red-and-yellow shoulder patches
12.childFriendlyNote: A black bird puffs up and flashes bright red shoulders while singing "conk-la-reee!". He's the boss of the marsh

12.description: Maple sugaring season in full flow. Warm days and freezing nights keep sap running, sugar shacks steaming
12.childFriendlyNote: The maple trees are giving their sweetest sap right now, drip, drip, drip into the buckets!

12.description: Pussy willow catkins soft and silver along streams, one of the first signs of approaching spring
12.childFriendlyNote: Stroke the fuzzy silver buds gently. They feel like the softest fur!

12.description: Snow still very possible in mid-March. Nor'easters can bring major storms, but snow melts faster now
12.childFriendlyNote: March can still surprise us with a big snowstorm! But the sun is strong enough to melt it faster

13.description: Red-winged blackbirds in full song at every marsh and pond edge, a sure sign of spring approaching
13.childFriendlyNote: Every marsh is ringing with "conk-la-reee!". The blackbirds are telling winter to go away

13.description: Late-season maple sugaring, sap running on warm days. Season ends when buds swell
13.childFriendlyNote: The maple syrup season is almost over. Once tree buds swell, the sap tastes bad

13.description: Pussy willow catkins fully expanded, some turning yellow with pollen
13.childFriendlyNote: The fuzzy silver catkins are getting bigger and turning golden. That's pollen!

13.description: Robins becoming more visible on lawns as snow melts, hopping and listening for worms
13.childFriendlyNote: Robins tilt their heads on the lawn. They're actually listening for worms underground!

13.description: Skunk cabbage leaves unfurling from hoods, bright green against brown wetland floor
13.childFriendlyNote: The skunk cabbage is unrolling big green leaves now. They'll get as big as elephant ears!

14.description: Coltsfoot blooming on roadsides and disturbed ground. Yellow daisy-like flowers appear before leaves
14.childFriendlyNote: Little yellow flowers pop up on bare roadsides. The leaves don't come until later, like a backwards plant!

14.description: First spring peepers calling from vernal pools on warm evenings: a high-pitched chorus of tiny tree frogs
14.childFriendlyNote: Tiny frogs the size of your thumb make a huge noise at night, "peep! peep! peep!" from every puddle

14.description: Red maple buds swelling, tiny red flowers beginning to open, the first tree to bloom
14.childFriendlyNote: Look up at the red maple. Tiny red flowers make the treetop glow pink before any leaves appear

14.description: Wood frogs thawing from their frozen state, migrating to vernal pools to breed, explosive breeding events
14.childFriendlyNote: This frog was frozen solid all winter! It thaws out and hops to a pond to lay eggs, amazing!

14.description: Robins arriving in numbers, singing at dawn, hopping on thawing lawns
14.childFriendlyNote: Robins are everywhere now! They sing "cheerily, cheer-up, cheerily" at sunrise

15.description: Spring peeper chorus intensifying on warm evenings, deafening near vernal pools and wetlands
15.childFriendlyNote: The peeper chorus is so loud you can't hear each other talk! All from frogs smaller than a grape

15.description: Forsythia bursting into golden-yellow bloom along fences and in gardens: a hallmark of early spring
15.childFriendlyNote: Bushes explode with yellow flowers before any leaves appear, like golden fireworks!

15.description: Crocuses and snowdrops blooming in gardens, purple, white and yellow cups opening in sunny spots
15.childFriendlyNote: Little cups of purple and gold pop open in the sun. They close up at night like sleepy flowers

15.description: Osprey returning to nest platforms and dead trees near water, carrying sticks to rebuild nests
15.childFriendlyNote: The fish hawk is back! It builds a huge stick nest and dives feet-first into the water to catch fish

15.description: Red maple in full bloom, fuzzy red flowers giving treetops a rosy glow against grey sky
15.childFriendlyNote: The treetops are blushing pink! Tiny red flowers bloom before any leaves: the first tree to show spring

16.description: Forsythia in full golden bloom, hedges and gardens lit up with yellow
16.childFriendlyNote: The yellow forsythia bushes are glowing like little suns in every garden!

16.description: Spring peeper chorus at full volume, deafening near any wetland on warm evenings
16.childFriendlyNote: Stand near a pond at sunset and close your eyes. The peeper chorus is like a wall of sound!

16.description: Woodcock performing aerial courtship displays at dusk. Listen for "peent" calls from open fields
16.childFriendlyNote: A chubby bird goes "peent!" then spirals up into the sky doing loop-the-loops in the dark!

16.description: Crocuses in full bloom in gardens and parks, honeybees visiting on warm afternoons
16.childFriendlyNote: Purple and yellow crocuses are wide open. Watch for the first bees of spring visiting them!

16.description: Daffodil shoots emerging, green spears poking through soil in gardens and along roadsides
16.childFriendlyNote: Green swords push up through the soil. They're getting ready to burst into golden trumpets soon

17.description: Daffodils beginning to bloom in sheltered spots, golden trumpets nodding in spring breeze
17.childFriendlyNote: The first golden daffodils are opening their trumpets. Spring is really here!

17.description: Forsythia fading as leaves begin to emerge, petals dropping
17.childFriendlyNote: The forsythia petals are falling like yellow confetti as green leaves take their place

17.description: Wood frog egg masses visible in vernal pools, jelly-like clumps the size of softballs
17.childFriendlyNote: Look in puddles in the woods for jelly blobs full of tiny black dots. Those are frog eggs!

17.description: Robins singing dawn chorus, pulling worms from thawing lawns, beginning to build nests
17.childFriendlyNote: Watch a robin tug a long worm out of the ground. Sometimes they have a tug-of-war!

17.description: Red maple flowers fading, tiny red winged seeds (samaras) beginning to develop
17.childFriendlyNote: The red maple flowers are turning into tiny helicopter seeds. They'll spin when they fall!

18.description: Daffodils at peak bloom across New England, golden trumpets in gardens, parks, and along roadsides
18.childFriendlyNote: Daffodils are everywhere! Golden trumpets nodding in the breeze like a brass band

18.description: Shadbush blooming white along woodland edges and streams: blooms when shad fish run upriver
18.childFriendlyNote: Delicate white flowers appear on small trees near streams. They bloom when a fish called shad swims upstream!

18.description: Ornamental cherry trees beginning to bloom in parks and gardens, pink and white clouds of petals
18.childFriendlyNote: Cherry trees burst into pink and white clouds. Stand under one when petals fall like snow!

18.description: Tree swallows returning, iridescent blue-green birds swooping over fields and ponds catching insects
18.childFriendlyNote: Shiny blue-green birds zoom over the pond catching bugs in mid-air. They never miss!

18.description: Fiddlehead ferns beginning to unfurl along streams and in moist woodlands: tightly coiled green spirals
18.childFriendlyNote: Curled-up baby ferns look just like the scroll at the top of a violin. They uncurl as they grow!

19.description: Early warblers arriving: yellow-rumped warblers, pine warblers, and palm warblers leading the wave
19.childFriendlyNote: Tiny colourful birds are arriving from Central America! They flew thousands of miles to get here

19.description: Cherry and crabapple trees in full bloom, petals drifting in the breeze
19.childFriendlyNote: Pink and white petals fall like confetti when the wind blows, spring snowflakes!

19.description: Daffodils still blooming, tulips emerging, gardens filling with colour
19.childFriendlyNote: Daffodils are starting to droop but tulips are popping up to take their place!

19.description: Shadbush in full white bloom along streams and woodland edges, a beacon of spring
19.childFriendlyNote: White-flowering shadbush trees glow at the edge of the woods like little ghosts

19.description: Fiddlehead ferns unfurling along stream banks: a popular spring foraging find in New England
19.childFriendlyNote: The fern spirals are uncurling! People in New England eat these. They taste like asparagus

20.description: Warbler migration intensifying: black-and-white warblers, black-throated green warblers, ovenbirds arriving
20.childFriendlyNote: More tiny colourful birds arriving every day. Look up in the treetops for flashes of yellow and green!

20.description: Baltimore orioles arriving, brilliant orange-and-black males singing from treetops
20.childFriendlyNote: A bird as orange as a flame perches in a tree and sings a beautiful flute song!

20.description: White and red trillium blooming on the forest floor, three petals, three leaves, a woodland treasure
20.childFriendlyNote: Everything about this flower comes in threes: three petals, three leaves, three sepals. Nature's magic number!

20.description: Apple orchards bursting into bloom, pink and white blossoms buzzing with bees
20.childFriendlyNote: Apple trees are covered in pink-white flowers. Every flower could become an apple if a bee visits!

20.description: First ruby-throated hummingbirds arriving, hovering at feeders and early flowers
20.childFriendlyNote: A tiny bird that hovers like a helicopter! Its wings beat 53 times per second, too fast to see

21.description: Peak warbler migration: magnolia, blackburnian, bay-breasted, Cape May warblers passing through, a birding spectacle
21.childFriendlyNote: This is the best week for warblers. Dozens of tiny colourful species stop in our trees on their way north!

21.description: Lilac buds swelling, earliest varieties beginning to open, fragrant purple and white clusters
21.childFriendlyNote: Lilac buds are getting fat and ready to pop. When they open, bury your nose in them for the best smell ever!

21.description: Orioles singing from treetops, building hanging basket nests, visiting orange halves and jelly feeders
21.childFriendlyNote: Put out half an orange and watch. The brilliant orange oriole loves oranges!

21.description: Apple orchards in full bloom, buzzing with honeybees and bumblebees pollinating
21.childFriendlyNote: Stand in an apple orchard and listen. It sounds like the whole orchard is humming with bees!

21.description: Hummingbirds established at feeders and visiting columbine and honeysuckle flowers
21.childFriendlyNote: The hummingbird sticks its long tongue deep into flowers to drink nectar, like drinking through a straw!

22.description: Lilacs in full bloom across New England, heavy fragrant clusters of purple, white, and pink
22.childFriendlyNote: Bury your nose in a lilac. It's the most amazing smell! New England is famous for its lilacs

22.description: Tail end of warbler migration, some species still passing through, breeding residents settling in to sing
22.childFriendlyNote: The last warblers are passing through. The ones that stay will start building nests

22.description: Pink lady's slipper orchids blooming in acidic woodlands under pines, a rare New England treasure
22.childFriendlyNote: A wild orchid shaped like a tiny pink slipper! It's rare and special. Look but don't pick!

22.description: Gray catbirds singing from dense shrubs, making cat-like mewing calls mixed with complex song
22.childFriendlyNote: A grey bird that sounds like a cat! It hides in bushes and goes "meow!" to trick you

22.description: Luna moths emerging, large pale green moths with long tail streamers, attracted to lights at night
22.childFriendlyNote: A huge pale green moth with long tails. It looks like a fairy! Check near porch lights at night

23.description: First fireflies blinking in meadows and gardens at dusk. Males flash to attract females
23.childFriendlyNote: Living lanterns float in the dark! Each flash is a firefly saying "here I am!" to find a friend

23.description: Lilacs in late bloom, fragrance still heavy in the air, petals beginning to drop
23.childFriendlyNote: Enjoy the last of the lilac smell. The petals are starting to fall like tiny purple snowflakes

23.description: Beach roses beginning to bloom along the coast, large pink flowers with intense fragrance
23.childFriendlyNote: Big pink roses grow right on the beach! Smell their sweet scent mixed with salty sea air

23.description: Catbirds singing complex songs from dense shrubs, mimicking other birds mixed with cat-like mewing
23.childFriendlyNote: The catbird copies other birds' songs and mixes them all together. It's a bird DJ!

23.description: Mountain laurel buds swelling in woodlands, Connecticut's state flower preparing to bloom
23.childFriendlyNote: Pink and white buds look like tiny ornaments on an evergreen bush. They'll pop open into stars!

24.description: Firefly displays increasing in meadows and backyards: magical blinking lights at dusk
24.childFriendlyNote: More fireflies every night! Watch their patterns. Different species flash in different rhythms

24.description: Beach roses in full bloom along the coast, large pink and white flowers humming with bees
24.childFriendlyNote: The beach is perfumed with roses! Big pink flowers grow right in the sand dunes

24.description: Mountain laurel blooming in woodlands, clusters of pink-white cup-shaped flowers with stamens like springs
24.childFriendlyNote: Each flower has tiny springs inside. When a bee lands, they fling pollen at it! Touch one gently and watch

24.description: Terns nesting on beaches and islands, diving headfirst into water for fish
24.childFriendlyNote: Sleek white birds hover over the water then plunge in headfirst. Splash! They almost never miss a fish

24.description: Lady's slipper orchids in bloom in pine and oak woodlands, delicate pink pouches on slender stems
24.childFriendlyNote: A wild orchid shaped like Cinderella's slipper! It takes 15 years to grow from seed to flower

25.description: Peak firefly season, meadows and gardens sparkling with hundreds of blinking lights at dusk
25.childFriendlyNote: This is the best week for fireflies! Go outside at dusk and count how many you can see

25.description: Milkweed plants growing tall with round pink flower clusters, essential food for monarch butterflies
25.childFriendlyNote: This plant has milky sap inside and sweet-smelling pink ball flowers. It's the only food baby monarch butterflies eat!

25.description: Lupines blooming in fields and along roadsides, tall spikes of purple, pink, and white, especially in Maine
25.childFriendlyNote: Tall spikes of purple flowers fill whole fields. Maine roads look like they have a purple carpet!

25.description: Beach plum in bloom along the coast, small white flowers on low bushes near dunes
25.childFriendlyNote: Small white flowers on the beach will become little plums in September. People make them into jelly!

25.description: Barn swallows swooping over fields and ponds, building mud nests under eaves and bridges
25.childFriendlyNote: Swallows scoop up mud in their beaks and build nests one mudball at a time, like tiny bricklayers!

26.description: Firefly displays still strong in late June evenings across meadows and gardens
26.childFriendlyNote: Fireflies are still putting on their light show! Each kind has its own flash pattern

26.description: Milkweed flowers opening, round clusters of fragrant pink-purple blooms attracting butterflies and bees
26.childFriendlyNote: Milkweed flowers smell sweet like candy! Butterflies and bees can't resist visiting

26.description: Horseshoe crabs spawning on Cape Cod and southern New England beaches during high tides
26.childFriendlyNote: Ancient creatures older than dinosaurs crawl onto the beach to lay eggs! They look like helmets with tails

26.description: Lupine fields still in bloom in northern New England and Maine, a spectacular sight
26.childFriendlyNote: Fields of purple lupines stretch as far as you can see, like something from a fairy tale

26.description: Wild strawberries ripening in sunny meadows and woodland edges, tiny but intensely flavoured
26.childFriendlyNote: Tiny red strawberries hiding in the grass. They're smaller than your thumbnail but taste amazing!

27.description: Milkweed in full bloom, monarch butterflies laying eggs on leaves, caterpillars beginning to hatch
27.childFriendlyNote: Look under milkweed leaves for tiny white eggs. A monarch butterfly left them there!

27.description: Wild lowbush blueberries beginning to ripen in rocky, sandy areas and barrens, a New England treasure
27.childFriendlyNote: Tiny wild blueberries are turning from green to blue! Maine's wild blueberries are the best in the world

27.description: Firefly displays beginning to slow as the season peaks and passes
27.childFriendlyNote: Enjoy the fireflies while they last. They'll start to fade as summer goes on

27.description: Barn swallows feeding young in nests, swooping low over fields catching insects
27.childFriendlyNote: Baby swallows poke their heads out of mud nests and beg for food. The parents work so hard!

27.description: Terns actively nesting on beaches, fiercely defending chicks, diving at intruders
27.childFriendlyNote: Don't get too close to tern nests. Angry parents will dive-bomb your head!

28.description: Monarch caterpillars growing on milkweed, bold yellow, black, and white stripes warning predators
28.childFriendlyNote: Stripy caterpillars munch milkweed leaves. Their bright colours say "don't eat me, I taste terrible!"

28.description: Wild blueberries ripening, sweet and ready to pick in barrens and rocky areas
28.childFriendlyNote: Wild blueberries are ripe! They're smaller than store ones but much sweeter and more flavourful

28.description: Black-eyed Susans blooming in meadows and roadsides, golden petals with dark brown centres
28.childFriendlyNote: Yellow flowers with dark centres look like little suns with eyes staring at you!

28.description: Dragonflies patrolling over ponds and meadows: iridescent hunters catching mosquitoes on the wing
28.childFriendlyNote: Dragonflies are like tiny helicopters. They can fly forward, backward, and even hover! They eat mosquitoes

28.description: Beach roses still blooming on the coast, beginning to form orange-red rose hips
28.childFriendlyNote: Beach roses are starting to make fat orange fruits called rose hips. Birds love them!

29.description: Monarch caterpillars getting large on milkweed, some forming chrysalises, jade green with gold dots
29.childFriendlyNote: The caterpillar hangs upside down and turns into a jewel-green case with gold spots. Magic is happening inside!

29.description: Peak wild blueberry season in Maine and across New England, picking time
29.childFriendlyNote: It's blueberry picking time! Your fingers will turn purple but your tummy will be happy

29.description: Black-eyed Susans and daisies blooming in meadows, filling roadsides with gold
29.childFriendlyNote: Fields of golden flowers with dark eyes nodding in the summer breeze

29.description: Dog-day cicadas buzzing from trees: loud droning sound on hot summer afternoons
29.childFriendlyNote: That loud buzzing in the trees? It's a cicada! They're as loud as a lawnmower but hard to find

29.description: Dragonflies in peak numbers, many species visible: green darners, blue dashers, twelve-spotted skimmers
29.childFriendlyNote: How many different coloured dragonflies can you spot? Blue, green, red. They're like flying jewels!

30.description: First generation monarch butterflies emerging from chrysalises, visiting milkweed and other flowers
30.childFriendlyNote: Brand new monarchs are emerging! Watch one unfold its crumpled wings and dry them in the sun

30.description: Cicadas droning loudly from treetops on hot days, the soundtrack of midsummer
30.childFriendlyNote: The trees are buzzing! Cicadas make the loudest sound of any insect. Find their empty shells on tree trunks

30.description: Black-eyed Susans, Queen Anne's lace, and chicory blooming in meadows and roadsides
30.childFriendlyNote: Golden black-eyed Susans and white Queen Anne's lace make roadside bouquets

30.description: Late blueberry picking, season winding down in southern New England but still good in Maine
30.childFriendlyNote: Last chance for blueberries in many places. But Maine still has plenty!

30.description: Green herons hunting along pond edges, crouching motionless then striking at fish and frogs
30.childFriendlyNote: A small heron crouches perfectly still then (snap!) catches a fish faster than you can blink

31.description: Monarchs nectaring on milkweed, bee balm, and coneflowers, building strength for eventual migration
31.childFriendlyNote: Monarchs are sipping nectar to fuel up. Some of their grandchildren will fly to Mexico!

31.description: Cicadas at peak volume on hot August days, empty exoskeletons clinging to tree bark
31.childFriendlyNote: Find cicada shells on tree trunks. The bug crawled out the back and left its skin behind like a ghost!

31.description: Early goldenrod beginning to bloom in meadows: golden plumes that signal summer's peak
31.childFriendlyNote: Golden fuzzy flowers are starting to appear in the fields. Summer is at its highest!

31.description: Hummingbirds very active at feeders and flowers, fattening up before fall migration
31.childFriendlyNote: Hummingbirds are eating extra now. They need to double their weight before flying south!

31.description: Joe-Pye weed blooming tall in wet meadows, dusty pink flower clusters attracting butterflies
31.childFriendlyNote: Tall pink flowers that butterflies love, named after a man who used it as medicine long ago

32.description: Goldenrod blooming across meadows, humming with bees and beetles, a sign of late summer
32.childFriendlyNote: Fields of gold! Goldenrod doesn't cause allergies. That's ragweed's fault, not goldenrod's

32.description: Monarchs still breeding, later-generation caterpillars on milkweed preparing for the great migration
32.childFriendlyNote: The monarchs being born now are the special ones. They'll live 8 months and fly to Mexico!

32.description: Nighthawks beginning to gather for migration, swooping over cities at dusk catching insects
32.childFriendlyNote: Bird-shaped silhouettes swoop over buildings at sunset. They catch bugs with their wide open mouths!

32.description: First New England asters beginning to bloom: purple and pink daisy-like flowers in meadows
32.childFriendlyNote: Purple star-shaped flowers are named after New England! They feed butterflies getting ready to migrate

32.description: Katydids calling "katy-did, katy-didn't" from treetops on warm August nights
32.childFriendlyNote: Listen at night. Bugs in the trees argue "katy-did! katy-didn't!" back and forth all night long

33.description: Goldenrod at peak bloom, meadows glowing gold, swarming with pollinators
33.childFriendlyNote: Every meadow is golden! Count how many different insects visit one goldenrod flower in a minute

33.description: Migration-generation monarchs emerging. These are the super-generation that will fly to Mexico
33.childFriendlyNote: These special monarchs will live 8 months and fly 3,000 miles to Mexico: the trip of a lifetime!

33.description: Nighthawk flocks migrating, sometimes dozens visible swooping over towns at dusk
33.childFriendlyNote: Look up at sunset for flocks of swooping nighthawks. They're heading south!

33.description: Katydids and crickets creating a loud nighttime chorus, the sound of late summer
33.childFriendlyNote: Summer nights are loud with bugs singing! Crickets chirp faster when it's warm. Count the chirps!

33.description: Cranberry bogs turning from green to red in Massachusetts and Cape Cod, harvest approaching
33.childFriendlyNote: Cranberry bogs are starting to turn red! Massachusetts grows tons of cranberries in flooded fields

34.description: Goldenrod and New England asters painting meadows gold and purple, late summer's colour palette
34.childFriendlyNote: Gold and purple flowers fill every field, like nature painted with autumn's colours early

34.description: Early monarch migration beginning: butterflies heading southwest, nectaring on goldenrod and asters
34.childFriendlyNote: Monarchs are starting their epic journey to Mexico! Watch them flutter south along the coast

34.description: Large nighthawk flocks migrating over cities and towns in the evening
34.childFriendlyNote: Dozens of nighthawks swoop together. They look like boomerangs flying through the sunset

34.description: First red maples beginning to show colour: isolated branches turning scarlet in swamps
34.childFriendlyNote: The first red maple leaves are turning red! Red maple is always the first tree to change colour

34.description: Field crickets chirping from every meadow and garden. Their song changes speed with temperature
34.childFriendlyNote: Count cricket chirps in 14 seconds and add 40. That's the temperature in Fahrenheit! Nature's thermometer

35.description: Goldenrod and New England asters at peak, meadows ablaze with gold and purple
35.childFriendlyNote: The last big flower show of the year! Gold and purple everywhere you look

35.description: Monarch migration strengthening, butterflies gathering in coastal areas before heading south
35.childFriendlyNote: Monarchs gather on the coast for their big trip, sometimes hundreds on one tree!

35.description: Red maples showing more autumn colour, scattered scarlet in swamps and along roads
35.childFriendlyNote: More red leaves appearing! Red maples turn colour weeks before other trees

35.description: Cranberry bogs deepening to red, harvest preparations beginning on Cape Cod
35.childFriendlyNote: The cranberry bogs look like red carpets! Soon farmers will flood them and the berries will float

35.description: Cricket chorus still strong but slowing as nights cool. A slower tempo signals autumn
35.childFriendlyNote: The crickets are singing more slowly now. Cooler nights make them chirp slower

36.description: Peak monarch migration through New England. Look for butterflies heading southwest along coast and ridgelines
36.childFriendlyNote: This is the best time to watch monarchs migrate! They follow the coast south toward Mexico

36.description: Fall warbler migration beginning. Confusing fall plumage makes identification a fun challenge
36.childFriendlyNote: Warblers are heading south in their dull autumn clothes. Even experts have trouble telling them apart!

36.description: Goldenrod beginning to go to seed, fluffy seed heads forming, still attracting late pollinators
36.childFriendlyNote: Goldenrod flowers are turning to fluffy seeds. Blow on them and watch them drift away

36.description: Red maples turning scarlet in earnest, bright against still-green oaks and birches
36.childFriendlyNote: Red maples are on fire! They're the first trees to show us that autumn is coming

36.description: Cranberry harvest beginning, bogs flooded and berries floating to the surface in a sea of red
36.childFriendlyNote: Farmers flood the cranberry bogs and the red berries float to the top. It looks like a red lake!

37.description: Northern New England (Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine mountains) showing first colour: red maples, sumac turning
37.childFriendlyNote: The northern mountains are starting to glow! Red, orange, and yellow are creeping down from the peaks

37.description: Monarchs still migrating through, nectaring on asters and goldenrod for fuel
37.childFriendlyNote: Wave goodbye to the last monarchs, next stop: Mexico, 3,000 miles away!

37.description: Fall warbler migration in full swing: mixed flocks moving through treetops
37.childFriendlyNote: Flocks of little birds hop through the treetops together: safety in numbers for the long trip south!

37.description: Broad-winged hawks beginning southward migration, riding thermals in kettles of dozens or hundreds
37.childFriendlyNote: Look up! Dozens of hawks circle together in the sky like a swirling funnel. They're riding warm air south

37.description: Woolly bear caterpillars crossing roads and paths, fuzzy black and brown banded caterpillars
37.childFriendlyNote: Fuzzy brown and black caterpillars are everywhere! Legend says their stripes predict how harsh winter will be

38.description: Fall colour spreading south from northern mountains: sugar maples, red maples, birches turning
38.childFriendlyNote: The hills are on fire with colour! Red, orange, yellow, like nature is painting with all the colours

38.description: Peak broad-winged hawk migration, kettles of hundreds visible from ridgelines and hawk-watch sites
38.childFriendlyNote: Hundreds of hawks spiral up together in the sky! Go to a hilltop and look south for the swirling funnels

38.description: Woolly bear caterpillars very active, crossing roads looking for places to hibernate for winter
38.childFriendlyNote: Help woolly bears cross the road safely! They curl into a ball when scared, so fuzzy and cute

38.description: White-throated sparrows arriving from the north, singing "Old Sam Peabody Peabody Peabody"
38.childFriendlyNote: A stripy sparrow sings "Oh sweet Canada Canada Canada". It's coming south for winter!

38.description: New England asters at peak bloom, vivid purple flowers providing last nectar for migrating butterflies
38.childFriendlyNote: Purple asters are the last flowers feeding butterflies before winter, nature's farewell feast!

39.description: Peak fall colour in Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine: sugar maples golden-orange, red maples scarlet, birches yellow
39.childFriendlyNote: This is it: the most colourful week of the year up north! Every tree is a different colour

39.description: Sharp-shinned hawks and Cooper's hawks migrating, smaller accipiters darting through woods
39.childFriendlyNote: Smaller hawks zoom through the trees like fighter jets. They're speedy little hunters

39.description: White-throated sparrows now common in thickets and at feeders, whistling their sweet song
39.childFriendlyNote: These stripy sparrows are winter visitors. They sing a beautiful whistle song even in the cold

39.description: Witch hazel beginning to bloom, spidery yellow flowers on bare branches, the last native shrub to flower
39.childFriendlyNote: A bush that blooms when everything else is dropping leaves! Yellow spidery flowers appear in autumn

39.description: Woolly bear caterpillars still crossing paths, seeking sheltered spots to spend winter
39.childFriendlyNote: Last chance to spot woolly bears. They'll soon hide under logs and leaves to sleep all winter

40.description: Peak fall colour reaching Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts: sugar maples, red oaks, hickories ablaze
40.childFriendlyNote: Now the southern towns are on fire with colour! Collect the most colourful leaf you can find

40.description: Witch hazel in bloom, spidery yellow flowers brightening the understory as other leaves fall
40.childFriendlyNote: The only bush still blooming! Its yellow spidery flowers glow in the bare autumn woods

40.description: White-throated sparrows abundant at feeders and in leaf litter, scratching for seeds
40.childFriendlyNote: White-throated sparrows scratch in the fallen leaves like they're playing in a ball pit!

40.description: Dark-eyed juncos returning from the north, "snowbirds" arriving to spend winter in New England
40.childFriendlyNote: The snowbirds are back! Little grey-and-white juncos hop under feeders all winter

40.description: Chipmunks frantically gathering and storing acorns and nuts before winter hibernation
40.childFriendlyNote: Chipmunks stuff their cheeks so full of acorns they can barely see! They're stocking their underground pantry

41.description: Fall colour past peak in the north, still vivid in southern New England: oaks holding bronze and russet leaves
41.childFriendlyNote: The bright colours are fading to brown and rust. Oaks hold on to their leaves the longest

41.description: Witch hazel still blooming, bright against bare forest, seeds exploding audibly from pods
41.childFriendlyNote: Witch hazel shoots its seeds like tiny bullets. Listen for popping sounds in the quiet woods!

41.description: Juncos now common at feeders, flashing white outer tail feathers as they hop on the ground
41.childFriendlyNote: Juncos flash white tail feathers when they fly, like little semaphore flags!

41.description: Deer rut beginning: bucks with polished antlers active, rubs visible on small trees
41.childFriendlyNote: Deer with big antlers are rubbing trees and acting tough. It's their mating season!

41.description: Pine siskins arriving from the north in irruptive flocks, visiting feeders with goldfinches
41.childFriendlyNote: Tiny streaky birds with yellow wing flashes. They travel in big groups from the far north

42.description: Oak leaves turning russet and brown, beech leaves papery gold, bare branches emerging as canopy thins
42.childFriendlyNote: Leaves are crunching underfoot! Kick through a pile and listen to that amazing sound

42.description: Deer rut in full swing: bucks crossing roads, very active at dawn and dusk, be careful driving
42.childFriendlyNote: Deer are very busy and distracted right now. They might run across roads, so watch out!

42.description: Juncos in large flocks at feeders and on the ground, the most common winter bird
42.childFriendlyNote: Juncos are everywhere now! They're winter's most faithful feeder birds

42.description: Cardinals more visible as leaves fall, red males striking against grey-brown bare branches
42.childFriendlyNote: Now that the leaves have fallen, you can see the cardinal so clearly, a red jewel in bare branches

42.description: Chipmunks making final trips to stock burrows before settling in for winter dormancy
42.childFriendlyNote: Chipmunks are making their last grocery runs! Soon they'll curl up underground for a long winter nap

43.description: Most deciduous trees bare, revealing bird nests, squirrel dreys, and tree architecture against the sky
43.childFriendlyNote: Now you can see things hidden all summer: old bird nests, squirrel houses, and the amazing shapes of branches!

43.description: Peak deer rut: bucks aggressive, does being chased, increased road crossings at dawn and dusk
43.childFriendlyNote: Bucks are chasing does through the woods. Be extra careful near roads at sunrise and sunset!

43.description: Cardinals visiting feeders in pairs, red males and brown females against bare branches
43.childFriendlyNote: Mr and Mrs Cardinal come to the feeder together. She's brown with a red beak, he's all red

43.description: First snow flurries possible in late October, especially in the northern mountains and hills
43.childFriendlyNote: Is that snow? The first flurries might fly in October. Winter is sending a preview!

43.description: Blue jays busy caching acorns for winter, carrying them in their throat pouch to hide in the ground
43.childFriendlyNote: Blue jays carry up to 5 acorns at once. They hide them in the ground and remember where 70% of them are!

44.description: Bare deciduous trees stark against the sky, white pines and hemlocks standing green, late fall transition
44.childFriendlyNote: The difference between bare trees and green evergreens is amazing now: two kinds of trees, two strategies!

44.description: Juncos in steady flocks at feeders, scratching in leaf litter under bushes
44.childFriendlyNote: Juncos hop-hop-hop under the feeder picking up seeds. They're very polite birds!

44.description: Deer rut winding down, bucks still active but less aggressive, moving into winter range
44.childFriendlyNote: The deer are calming down after their busy mating season. Now they need to eat and rest

44.description: Cardinals bright at feeders, one of the most visible birds now that leaves have dropped
44.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal looks like a red ornament hanging in a bare tree, bright and beautiful against grey

44.description: Titmice visiting feeders with chickadees, caching seeds in bark crevices for winter
44.childFriendlyNote: The titmouse takes one seed at a time, flies away to hide it, then comes back for another: a very organised bird!

45.description: Chickadees in mixed flocks with titmice and nuthatches, visiting feeders frequently as days shorten
45.childFriendlyNote: Chickadees, titmice, and nuthatches travel together, a little bird gang keeping each other safe!

45.description: First measurable snow often falls in early November across New England, dusting the bare landscape
45.childFriendlyNote: The first real snow! Even a little dusting makes everything look magical and clean

45.description: Juncos settled into winter territories, large flocks at feeders and on snowy ground
45.childFriendlyNote: Juncos love scratching in the snow for seeds. They do a funny little hop-scratch dance!

45.description: Cardinals striking against first snow and bare branches, beginning quiet winter songs
45.childFriendlyNote: Red cardinal on white snow, one of the most beautiful sights in nature!

45.description: First thin ice forming on still ponds and puddles, crunchy underfoot in morning
45.childFriendlyNote: Step on thin ice on a puddle and hear it crackle! Watch ice crystals grow on the edges of ponds

46.description: Cardinals vivid at feeders, one of few bright colours in the November landscape
46.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal is like a splash of paint on a grey canvas, so bright against bare November trees

46.description: Chickadees cache seeds and remember thousands of hiding spots, remarkable winter survival strategy
46.childFriendlyNote: Chickadees hide seeds in thousands of places and remember each one! Their brains grow bigger in autumn to help

46.description: Nuthatches walking headfirst down tree trunks, finding insects other birds miss
46.childFriendlyNote: The nuthatch walks down trees upside-down and finds bugs that right-side-up birds missed!

46.description: Red-tailed hawks easily spotted perched on bare trees and poles, hunting over open fields
46.childFriendlyNote: With all the leaves gone, you can spot big hawks sitting in trees. Look for a big shape on a high branch

46.description: Grey overcast skies typical of November, early sunsets by 4:30pm, longest nights approaching
46.childFriendlyNote: The sun sets so early now! But that means more time to look for stars and constellations

47.description: Cardinals at feeders throughout the day, males sometimes giving quiet winter songs
47.childFriendlyNote: Even on the darkest November days, the cardinal brings colour and a quiet little song

47.description: Junco flocks at feeders, scratching in leaf litter and on frozen ground
47.childFriendlyNote: Juncos love to eat seeds right off the ground. Scatter some and watch them hop over!

47.description: Red-tailed hawks hunting from bare tree perches, easy to spot in leafless landscape
47.childFriendlyNote: Count how many hawks you spot on a car ride. With no leaves, every hawk perch is visible!

47.description: Eastern white pines and hemlocks vivid green against grey bare hardwoods: the backbone of the winter forest
47.childFriendlyNote: Evergreen trees are the heroes of winter! They stay green and give shelter to birds and animals

47.description: Ice thickening on ponds and puddles, frost on grass every morning, winter settling in
47.childFriendlyNote: The pond ice gets thicker every night, but it's not safe to walk on yet! Watch from the shore

48.description: Cardinals reliable at feeders as December approaches, often first bird at the feeder at dawn
48.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal is the early bird! It's usually the first one at the feeder every morning

48.description: Chickadees fluffing up to stay warm, looking like little round balls perched on branches
48.childFriendlyNote: Chickadees puff up into round fluffballs to trap warm air, like wearing a tiny down jacket!

48.description: Juncos in winter flocks, a constant presence at feeders and on snowy ground
48.childFriendlyNote: Juncos don't mind the cold! They sleep in thick bushes and come out to eat all day

48.description: Red-tailed hawks perched on bare trees, very visible in late November landscape
48.childFriendlyNote: A hawk sits on a bare branch, watching everything with sharp eyes. It can spot a mouse from 100 feet up!

48.description: First significant snow may have fallen, ponds freezing over, winter settling in across New England
48.childFriendlyNote: Winter is here! Look for animal tracks in the snow and frost patterns on windows

49.description: Cardinals bright red against fresh December snow, a classic New England winter scene
49.childFriendlyNote: Red cardinal on white snow looks like a holiday card come to life!

49.description: Chickadees retrieving cached seeds, their remarkable memory guiding them to thousands of hiding spots
49.childFriendlyNote: Now the chickadee eats the seeds it hid last autumn. It remembers where thousands of them are!

49.description: Great horned owls beginning courtship hooting, deep "hoo-hoo-hoooo" duets at dusk
49.childFriendlyNote: Listen at sunset for deep hooting. The owls are starting to sing love songs already!

49.description: White pines and hemlocks draped in snow, sheltering birds and deer beneath their boughs
49.childFriendlyNote: Under a big pine tree is like a tent. The snow can't get through and it smells like Christmas!

49.description: Days near their shortest: sunrise after 7am, sunset before 4:15pm, barely 9 hours of daylight
49.childFriendlyNote: The shortest day of the year is coming! After that, every day gets a tiny bit longer. The light returns

50.description: Winter solstice week, the shortest day and longest night of the year, about 9 hours of daylight
50.childFriendlyNote: The shortest day of the year! After today, each day gets a little longer. The sun is coming back!

50.description: Cardinals at feeders through the short winter days, red feathers glowing in low winter sun
50.childFriendlyNote: The cardinal never leaves us! It's here singing even on the darkest, coldest days

50.description: Great horned owls courting, hooting duets becoming more frequent as breeding season approaches
50.childFriendlyNote: Two owls sing to each other in the dark: "hoo-hoo" answers "hoo-hoo" like a conversation

50.description: Chickadees in mixed flocks, spending the short daylight hours feeding intensively
50.childFriendlyNote: Chickadees eat all day in winter. They need to or they won't make it through the long cold night

50.description: Snow covering the landscape, ponds frozen solid, icicles growing from eaves, deep winter beauty
50.childFriendlyNote: Everything is white and sparkling! Look for animal tracks telling stories in the fresh snow

51.description: Cardinals bright against snow and evergreens, a holiday icon of New England winter
51.childFriendlyNote: The red cardinal against white snow and green pine: nature's own holiday decoration!

51.description: Great horned owls courting intensely, may be selecting nest sites in bare trees
51.childFriendlyNote: Owls are picking out their nursery! They'll use an old hawk or crow nest and fix it up

51.description: Chickadees lively at feeders, their "chick-a-dee-dee" calls ringing through cold quiet woods
51.childFriendlyNote: Even in deep winter, the chickadee is cheerful! It's one of the bravest little birds

51.description: Fresh snow reveals a world of activity: deer, fox, rabbit, squirrel, and mouse tracks crisscrossing
51.childFriendlyNote: Snow is like a diary. Every animal writes its story with footprints! Can you read the tracks?

51.description: Titmice visiting feeders with chickadees and nuthatches, calling "peter-peter" from bare branches
51.childFriendlyNote: The titmouse is the chickadee's best friend. They travel together all winter!

52.description: Cardinals at feeders to close out the year, singing quietly even in deepest winter
52.childFriendlyNote: As the year ends, the cardinal is still here singing, a promise that spring will come again

52.description: Great horned owls hooting through long winter nights, courtship building toward January nesting
52.childFriendlyNote: The owl is planning a family! It hoots through the long cold night, getting ready to nest soon

52.description: Chickadees fluffed up at feeders, surviving deep cold by lowering their body temperature at night
52.childFriendlyNote: Chickadees let their body temperature drop at night to save energy, like turning down the thermostat!

52.description: Juncos in winter flocks, scratching at snowy ground under feeders and bushes
52.childFriendlyNote: Juncos are little snowbirds. They seem happiest when there's snow on the ground!

52.description: Deep New England winter: short days, long nights, snow-covered landscape, frozen ponds, bare hardwoods against grey sky
52.childFriendlyNote: The year ends in a hush of white, but underneath the snow, roots are waiting and days are getting longer!
